title: Executive Dysfunction Explained: The 7 Functions and ADHD
description:
Executive dysfunction is at the heart of ADHD — but most explanations stop at 'you have trouble focusing.' This video breaks down all 7 executive functions, what's actually happening in the ADHD brain for each one, and why standard advice so often fails. If you've ever felt like you knew exactly what you needed to do and still couldn't do it, this is for you. Keywords: executive dysfunction ADHD, ADHD executive function, ADHD brain explained, why ADHD makes tasks hard, ADHD prefrontal cortex.

Chapters:

chapters.title: It Is Not a Willpower Problem
chapters.voiceover: You know exactly what you need to do. You've known for three hours. The task is sitting right there — an email, a form, a single phone call that would take four minutes. And you cannot make yourself start. So you open the tab again. Close it. Make coffee you don't drink. And at some point a familiar thought creeps in: what is wrong with me? Here is what's actually wrong, and it is not what you think. It is not laziness. It is not a character flaw. It is not a question of caring enough. What you are experiencing has a name: executive dysfunction. And it is the single most disabling — and least understood — feature of ADHD. Executive functions are the brain's management system. They are a cluster of mental processes that live primarily in the prefrontal cortex, the region right behind your forehead. They handle things like starting tasks, holding information in mind, managing emotions, tracking time, and correcting your own behavior. In a brain with ADHD, these functions are not absent — they are dysregulated. The hardware exists. The connectivity is unreliable. This video is going to walk you through all seven executive functions, what the neuroscience actually says about each one, what it looks like in daily life, and what actually helps. Not 'just make a list.' Real strategies, grounded in how the ADHD brain works. Stay with me.

chapters.title: Inhibition: The Brake That Slips
chapters.voiceover: The first executive function is inhibition — and it is the foundation everything else rests on. Inhibition is the brain's ability to pause before acting, to filter out what isn't relevant, and to stop a behavior that isn't serving you. Think of it as the brake pedal. In ADHD, the brake is not broken — it just has very poor grip. Dr. Russell Barkley, one of the leading researchers in ADHD, argues that inhibition is the core deficit from which most other executive function problems flow. Here is what poor inhibition actually looks like: you are in a meeting and a thought arrives, completely unrelated, and it is out of your mouth before you registered deciding to say it. You sit down to do one thing and twenty minutes later you are deep in something entirely different with no memory of the transition. You feel an emotion — frustration, excitement, anxiety — and it is immediately, fully present, with no buffer between feeling and reaction. That buffer — that pause — is what inhibition creates. Neurologically, inhibition depends heavily on dopamine signaling in the prefrontal cortex. In ADHD brains, dopamine transmission is less efficient, meaning the signals that say 'wait, evaluate, then act' are quieter and slower than they need to be. The advice 'just think before you speak' or 'stop and consider your options' is not wrong — it just assumes the pause happens automatically. In ADHD, you have to build the pause deliberately. One method that works: a physical anchor. Before responding to anything — an email, a question, an impulse — press your feet flat into the floor for three seconds. That somatic cue is concrete enough to interrupt the automatic response chain and buy the cortex time to catch up.

chapters.title: Working Memory and Time: The Two That Hurt Most
chapters.voiceover: Working memory is your brain's mental whiteboard — the space where you hold information while you are actively using it. You walk into a room to get something. By the time you arrive, the something is gone. Someone gives you three instructions and you complete the first one perfectly and have no idea what the other two were. You are reading a paragraph and by sentence four you have lost sentence one. That is working memory under pressure. In ADHD, working memory capacity is measurably reduced. Research by Martinussen and colleagues found that children and adults with ADHD score significantly lower on working memory tasks, particularly ones involving verbal and spatial information held over time. This is not about intelligence. It is about RAM, not processing power. The whiteboard is smaller and it erases faster. The fix that doesn't work: 'just try to remember.' The fix that does: externalize everything. Working memory was never designed to be the only storage system — that's a modern expectation. Use a capture tool that is always with you, always frictionless. Not an app with seventeen steps to open — a physical sticky note on your desk, a voice memo button, one simple inbox. When a thought arrives, it goes there immediately, not in a second, not after you finish the sentence. Now — time. Time blindness is not a metaphor. Research using neuroimaging shows that ADHD brains have measurable differences in how they perceive duration. For neurotypical people, time feels like a river — always present, always moving. For many with ADHD, there are only two times: now, and not now. A deadline that is three weeks away is in the 'not now' pile until suddenly it is catastrophically now. Analog clocks — ones with hands — make time visible in a way digital clocks do not. Placing one in your line of sight is a small intervention with outsized impact because it makes the passage of time concrete rather than abstract.

chapters.title: Emotional Regulation and Motivation: The Hidden Core
chapters.voiceover: Here is one that does not make it into most ADHD explainers, and it should. Emotional dysregulation. ADHD is not classified as an emotional disorder, but Barkley and others argue it absolutely should involve emotion — because the prefrontal cortex does not just manage tasks. It manages the emotional responses that either fuel or derail those tasks. When the prefrontal cortex has weak inhibitory control, emotions arrive at full volume with no dimmer switch. Frustration becomes rage. Disappointment becomes devastation. Excitement becomes an all-consuming hyperfocus that crowds out everything else you were supposed to do. This is called low frustration tolerance, and it is biological, not dramatic. It is also deeply connected to motivation — specifically, how ADHD brains access dopamine-driven motivation. Neurotypical people can motivate themselves with future rewards: 'If I finish this report, I'll feel good about it later.' That future-state dopamine signal is enough to generate movement. In ADHD, the brain's reward system is less sensitive to delayed, abstract rewards. It responds strongly to things that are immediate, novel, interesting, or emotionally charged. This is why an ADHD person can spend six hours in hyperfocus on something they find genuinely interesting and cannot spend twenty minutes on something important but boring. Both are real. Neither is a choice. So the strategy is not to find more willpower — it is to engineer interest. Before a dreaded task, give yourself two minutes of something genuinely stimulating: a song that moves you, a brief physical reset, a voice note to a friend. You are not procrastinating. You are priming your dopamine system so the tank has something in it when you ask it to run.

chapters.title: Planning, Flexibility, and Self-Monitoring
chapters.voiceover: We are in the final three executive functions now, and they cluster together in a way that is worth understanding as a system. Planning and organization. Cognitive flexibility. And self-monitoring. Planning is the ability to break a large goal into sequenced steps and to estimate how long each step will take. For ADHD brains, both of these are genuinely hard. It is not that the goal is unclear — it is that the path between here and there is not automatically generated. You see the destination and you see where you are standing and the middle is fog. This is why 'just make a plan' fails: making a plan requires the same executive resources that are already strained. The workaround is not to plan more — it is to plan smaller. Instead of planning a project, plan only the next physical action. Not 'write the report' — 'open a new document and type one sentence.' The brain can find that. It cannot always find the full staircase, but it can find the next step. Cognitive flexibility is the ability to shift between tasks, rules, or mental frameworks without getting stuck. In ADHD, transitions are genuinely costly. Moving from one task to another — even a wanted task — requires effort that neurotypical people do not experience the same way. This is why interruptions are devastating and why being told to 'just switch gears' feels like being told to 'just land the plane.' A concrete help: transition warnings. Before a task needs to end, give yourself a five-minute heads-up, out loud or on a timer. Your brain needs a runway, not a cliff edge. Self-monitoring — the ability to observe your own behavior in real time and catch drift — is the last function, and arguably the most metacognitive. ADHD brains often miss the moment they got off track. The email that was open for forty minutes? At no point did a clear signal fire saying 'you have been doing this too long.' Regular external check-ins — a timer, a body-doubling partner, a simple hourly alarm — replace the internal signal that misfires.

chapters.title: What This All Means for You
chapters.voiceover: So here is the full picture. Seven executive functions — inhibition, working memory, time perception, emotional regulation, motivation, planning and flexibility, and self-monitoring — all relying on dopamine-sensitive prefrontal circuitry that, in ADHD, runs differently. Not worse as a person. Differently as a brain. And the reason this matters — the reason you needed to sit with all of this — is not so you have a better answer at trivia night. It is because shame is not a neutral experience. When you believe your inability to start a task is a moral failing, you add the cognitive and emotional weight of self-criticism to a brain that is already running with reduced resources. Research by Kristin Neff and others on self-compassion shows that self-criticism actually reduces performance and increases avoidance. Shame does not motivate the ADHD brain. It makes everything harder. Understanding the mechanism gives you something shame never could: a place to actually intervene. You are not trying to 'be better.' You are building external scaffolding for internal processes that need support. Capture tools for working memory. Analog clocks for time. Transition warnings for flexibility. Physical anchors for inhibition. Dopamine priming for motivation. Next-action planning for the fog. None of these are cheating. None of these are crutches. They are the equivalent of glasses for someone who cannot see the board. The board was never the problem. This is a long journey and one video is only a beginning — but you now know more about your own brain than most people ever will. That knowledge is the starting line. Follow for daily ADHD content — every video goes deeper.
